    #89701. Industry News: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1652 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In fresh research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    According to recent reports, the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Recent findings suggest that many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In a recent development, despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) stated they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    According to recent reports, our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more rapidly.

    “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) mentioned they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    In a recent development, using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) stated they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    Recent findings suggest that as AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    Sources indicate that as in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    According to recent reports, people across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    Industry observers note that this also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    According to recent reports, first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also highlights that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a newly introduced dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily customers and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.     ProcessOS is a new kind of Camunda product: business processes described in natural language, generated as executable BPMN workflows, and improved autonomously from production data. We’re hiring the first cohort of Forward Deployed Engineers to bring it into production at enterprise customers. You’ll own the deployment journey from first process file to a working, improving system, and hand off a functioning capability to the customer’s team. The code you write and the patterns you discover feed directly back into how ProcessOS is built. This is a rare opportunity to shape a product, a function, and a field practice from day one.

    You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.

    According to recent reports, deploy and prove. Own the journey from first process file to production workflow. At 90 days: at least one workflow running, the improvement loop active, and measurable fitness gains the customer can see. At 12 months: 3–5 customers with viable deployments.

    In a recent development, drive organizational adoption. Work across technical and business stakeholders to build understanding and trust, turning early deployments into lasting customer capability.

    Work at depth technically. Configure and run Camunda clusters locally and in cloud environments. Debug integration failures. Build custom agents where platform defaults don’t fit. Write connector logic that gets legacy enterprise systems talking to ProcessOS.

    Build the playbook. There is no deployment template yet. Document what good looks like as you discover it, and make the next implementation faster.

    Feed the product. Custom agents you write get contributed back. Integration patterns get codified. Production bugs you find, you often fix. Your field work is a direct input to ProcessOS.

    Hand off deliberately. Leave customers with a team that can operate independently, is trained on the platform, and acts on improvement results without you.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    Sources indicate that as pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and fresh hybrid work schedules.

    On Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

    I Blind-Tested 3 Gemini Models On Real SEO Questions – Neon Won 5 Of 6 via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.
    • Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s upcoming Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
    • Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

    Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s upcoming Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

    Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

    You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

    Recent findings suggest that the blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

    Sources indicate that my Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

    On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

    So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:.

    Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week blueprint that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

    With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

    When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:.

    Sources indicate that what stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

    Industry observers note that my revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):.

    Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

    Industry observers note that at first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a big jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active customers, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:.

    And those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions.
    • In a recent development, as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent.
    • It has been revealed that this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

    In a recent development, as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

    It has been revealed that this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

    You build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

    According to recent reports, this role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice.

    You'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

    It has been revealed that the operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

    Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end.

    Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live.

    Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff.

    Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip.

    Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production.

    Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work.

    Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM.

    Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild.

    Have taken one net-fresh agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner.

    Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change.

    Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you.

    Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field.

    Sources indicate that 7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). We do not count years of AI experience; the field is too young for that to mean anything. We look at what you have shipped and how you reason about it.

    Integration and API engineering: secure service-to-service endpoints, third-party APIs, webhooks, and the patience to work with legacy banking systems that were not designed to be integrated.

    According to recent reports, security and auth judgment: OAuth and machine-to-machine auth, tenant-scoped access, secrets handling, no PII in logs. Our agents touch sensitive member data and operate under consumer-contact regulation.

    It has been revealed that customer presence: you can sit across from a VP of Collections, hear a request, and say "here is what I recommend and why", including when the answer is no. You are comfortable making calls in the room and owning them afterwards.

    Code-quality judgment under deadline pressure: you take on debt deliberately, name it, and pay it down, rather than gold-plating or leaving silent debt behind.

    It has been revealed that genuine appetite for LLM agents: eval discipline for non-deterministic systems, reading a system prompt like code, understanding that some decisions must never reach the model. Curiosity plus shipped work is enough; research depth is not required.

    Nice to have, explicitly not required: voice and telephony (LiveKit, Twilio), Temporal or event-driven orchestration, Python, core banking or LOS integration experience, credit union or banking domain knowledge.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance aims.

    Sources indicate that clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS tech giant, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Tech Report: “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The fresh budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The fresh budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Industry observers note that expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan noted. “They see what Significant Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    According to recent reports, the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

    It has been revealed that there’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    According to recent reports, “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    In a recent development, in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Recent findings suggest that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Debuted in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    According to recent reports, even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he mentioned.

    Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    Industry observers note that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan stated. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • According to recent reports, the Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine.
    • Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    According to recent reports, the Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

    Salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

    Sources indicate that this role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical looks, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

    You understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

    You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:.

    Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

    Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

    Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

    Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

    Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

    Are a fast learner, frequently picking up new languages and tools.

    Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

    Own the architecture of the GTM systems stack: define how Salesforce, HubSpot, enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and the data platform fit together, and write the technical strategy that guides how it evolves.

    Lead build-vs-buy and procurement decisions: evaluate vendors, run proofs of concept, assess security and integration fit, and partner with Director of GTM Systems and Analytics, Finance, Legal, and IT on selection and renewals.

    Shape the GTM systems roadmap with senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, RevOps, Finance, and Engineering: align on requirements, sequence investments, make clear tradeoffs, and lead cross-functional initiatives to completion.

    Own Salesforce as the engineering system of record for revenue: data model, flows and automation, validation rules, field governance, and access control.

    Own HubSpot for campaigns and lead generation, along with the HubSpot-Salesforce sync — so leads, contacts, and engagement signals reach the revenue pipeline without drift or silent failures.

    Build and maintain integrations across the GTM stack, and partner with GTM Analytics Engineering on reliable data flows to the central data platform.

    Design and deploy agentic workflows that consume GTM data, surface actionable signals, and automate manual operations — and set the patterns and guardrails others build on.

    Establish observability and change management for critical GTM systems: alerts, dashboards, and runbooks; reviewed code changes, documented config, and rollback paths.

    Mentor engineers across experience levels and set the technical standards for the team.

    Partner with the Billing Systems Engineer to automate the CPQ-to-Billing handoff.

    Extensive engineering experience in GTM or business systems, including owning a GTM stack's architecture end to end — build-vs-buy calls, vendor evaluations, and systems designed for a multi-year horizon.

    According to recent reports, deep, hands-on Salesforce expertise — you understand the data model, have built complex flows and automation, and you think about it as an engineering system, not an admin tool. This is the primary bar.

    HubSpot experience in a marketing context, including the HubSpot-Salesforce sync and what breaks and why.

    Technical depth beyond the UI — you've built integrations with APIs, webhooks, and event streams, and you know when a native tool (a Flow, a Clay table, a HubSpot workflow) is the right answer versus when it's time to write code.

    Agentic workflow experience — you've designed and deployed AI agents that act on GTM data in production.

    Strong change management practices — you've shipped changes to live systems while protecting active deals and campaigns.

    Experience influencing senior stakeholders — translating business strategy into system requirements and roadmaps.

    A history of mentoring engineers, from early-career to senior.

    Salesforce CPQ: approvals, order forms, discounting rules, and the closed-won-to-billing path.

    SQL and data modeling fluency; familiarity with a warehouse-centric stack (BigQuery, Snowflake, dbt, reverse ETL).

    Experience with billing platforms (Stripe, Zuora, Maxio) and the handoffs between GTM systems and billing.

    Experience managing a GTM tooling budget or vendor portfolio.

    Experience as a technical lead on a GTM or business systems team.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    Sources indicate that at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, increased hotel costs, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Recent findings suggest that revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that the Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five full-time staffers. Niketa Patel, the organization’s CEO and executive director, will stay on as ONA’s only full-time employee and will oversee the Women’s Leadership Accelerator program, online resources, and newsletters “with some assistance from a few consultants and volunteers,” she told me in an email.

    Sources indicate that “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Patel wrote in her ONA announcement. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    Industry observers note that LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    Industry observers note that LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson stated.

    OpenNews mentioned in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    Sources indicate that the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he remarked. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. (Patel, too, mentioned that 25% of ONA attendees were international and “many of these people have either not wanted to come to the U.S. or have been banned from doing so by their employers. Naturally, it makes sense for employers to protect their staff, given what we keep witnessing playing out on streets around the country.”) ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” This story has been updated with comment from ONA. a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone.

    IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March.

    The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year.

    But things have gotten harder, he remarked. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. (Patel, too, mentioned that 25% of ONA attendees were international and “many of these people have either not wanted to come to the U.S. or have been banned from doing so by their employers. Naturally, it makes sense for employers to protect their staff, given what we keep witnessing playing out on streets around the country.”) ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small.

    Reddit’s AEO Tool Recommendations Have A Promoter Problem via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Graphite flagged 55% of the owners who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.
    • Among the people it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.
    • The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Graphite flagged 55% of the owners who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

    Among the people it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

    The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

    Industry observers note that the agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and indicates it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

    Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

    A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

    It has been revealed that to test the model, the organization manually inspected 43 of the users it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also says that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

    Sources indicate that four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

    Sources indicate that one account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

    Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

    A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

    In a recent development, over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

    Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from owners who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

    Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from people it flagged as likely promoters.

    It has been revealed that according to the write-up, users frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

    It has been revealed that the citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by users. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

    Sources indicate that the agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also noted the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

    In a recent development, graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit owners weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

    According to recent reports, graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the company says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

    According to recent reports, this is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. Together with the RevOps team, you own the shared language of the business (definitions, data, and processes) so commercial teams make decisions from one view of it.

    When something important doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a new commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership. This is a fast-moving startup. We're building toward a much larger firm but we aren't one yet, and most of this role has no playbook. You'll define the process, build the tool, and hand it to the team. If you want established structure, this likely isn't the role.

    You'll report to the Director of Business Operations and work directly with senior leaders across the company as a neutral partner to every function rather than an advocate for one. Your work will be visible, and it will significantly influence how we make commercial decisions.

    According to recent reports, you'll lead a small, high-ownership RevOps team that runs the systems and data our commercial teams depend on, and creates leverage for them to do their jobs even better. The team doesn't just own systems. They build automation, tooling, and processes, and they're close partners to Sales and Marketing. You'll coach them, set priorities, and open up more strategic scope, while giving them real autonomy.

    Learn the business end to end: the revenue funnel, the customer lifecycle, how each commercial team works day to day, and where decisions get stuck.

    Build trust with your RevOps team: learn the work they own, and set priorities and team rhythms together.

    Deliver the first version of client-level margin and cost-to-serve, the analysis that grounds our pricing strategy.

    Develop a first point of view on pricing and packaging for revenue leadership, built on that analysis.

    Put AI to work in your own workflow from week one, and identify the first set of manual, repetitive processes across the commercial teams worth automating.

    Stand up a first version of a deal desk, including an approval workflow, pricing and discount guardrails, and standard commercial terms.

    Partner with Sales and Marketing leaders as they prepare for the monthly business review: pressure-test their aims and point out risks, then solve them with the RevOps team by creating upcoming processes, tooling, or automation.

    Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

    Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

    Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

    Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

    Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next notable thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

    5-8 years of total experience that combines consulting or banking with time as an operator inside a manufacturer.

    Experience managing people: you've coached ICs, given direct feedback, made tough talent calls, and built team rhythms.

    According to recent reports, startup experience. You've worked in a fast-moving, ever-changing environment where structure wasn't already there, and you built it. This is not a role for someone whose experience is only at large, established enterprises.

    Strong analytical and financial modeling skills, including forecasting. You're very comfortable building models in spreadsheets from scratch, and they hold up to scrutiny. You use AI to move faster and sharpen your work, and you have the foundational modeling knowledge to know when its output is wrong.

    It has been revealed that data-first and self-sufficient. You open the dataset before you build the slide, you're always looking for more data to test an idea, and you're comfortable getting into raw data yourself. You use AI to analyze it faster and know enough to check its work.

    Commercial acumen: you can read commercial terms, spot the problematic ones, and reason about pricing, discounting, margin, and deal structure.

    A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

    Comfort with ambiguity. When something isn't set up yet, your instinct is to build it, not to wait for it. You create structure, manage competing priorities, and pivot when things change.

    Relentless follow-through: you close loops, and people stop checking on what you've noted you'll do.

    A partner's temperament: you challenge constructively without taking sides, you surface problems early, and you resolve cross-team conflict without escalating it.

    Industry experience in fintech, financial services, lending, banking, or credit unions.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance plans.

    It has been revealed that clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS firm, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

    Industry observers note that any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

    Industry observers note that back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content.     #89681. Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature.
    • Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.
    • Sources indicate that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature. The expansion unifies many of Google’s disparate products and services into a single personalized search experience. This upgrade represents a profound change to Google’s Search experience and is likely among the most consequential changes to SEO.

    Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.

    Sources indicate that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we’re introducing more personally relevant responses, so it’s easier to find just what you need.”.

    Some SEOs objected to characterizing Personal Intelligence as something that is about Search, explaining that Personal Intelligence is about Gemini, AI Mode, and AI Overviews. That view can be justified because Google’s announcement is somewhat ambiguous.

    In a recent development, google’s announcement uses the upper-case word Search sixteen times. That seems to be a clear signal that Personal Intelligence affects Search.

    “A more tailored Google Search that’s uniquely yours….

    …Get more helpful Search responses….

    …Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence….

    …bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The following passage seems to unambiguously paint the rollout as affecting Search:.

    “Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The above passage clearly separates AI Mode from Search. Yet, other passages reference AI Mode in Search, introducing a certain amount of ambiguity. An argument can be made that this does not affect Search, but there’s a strong counter-argument there, too.

    Google’s announcement ties AI Overviews and AI Mode responses to recent Search contexts, meaning that contextual data from Search can be shared to AIO and AI Mode:.

    “You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context.”.

    And in another passage Google explains that the contextual data from the Gemini App can be shared with AI Mode in Search:.

    “In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.”.

    “So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.”.

    So it looks like the context data flows from Search to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as from the Gemini App to AI Mode in Search.

    The announcement identifies six connected apps:.

    In a recent development, but Personal Intelligence is about a whole lot more. It’s about the transformation of disparate services and products into what Google CEO, Sundar Pichai, described in October 2026 as one unified search experience that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

    Recent findings suggest that “I expect our agents to provide that unifying experience across these products. In fact, that agentic layer, rather than try to converge or think about different products and how they come together, I think the agentic layer naturally ends up doing that, right?

    Sources indicate that because your agents, they’re running in the cloud, they’re running 24/7, they have your context. And so they can pick up things where you left off.

    So you can start a task in some place. You go to the other place. Your agent has that context for you.

    So I think the agentic layer offers us a chance to bring a unified product experience better than ever before.”.

    Google’s Personal Intelligence was first declared as a paid Gemini App beta feature in January 2026, which was expanded to AI Mode in search about a week later, initially supporting Gmail and Google Photos as an opt-in Search Labs experiment.

    In March it was expanded to free tier users in the United States and within a few months it was available in 200 countries and 98 languages.

    Recent findings suggest that google declared the expansion of the range of information AI Mode can draw on through Personal Intelligence so that now it includes Google Wallet data, files stored in Google Drive, and Gemini conversations. Google also announced increased personalization of AI Overviews and AI Mode based on recent search activity.

    Opt-in connectivity of Google Wallet to AI Mode is beginning to roll out. This is really big and ties into Sundar Pichai’s vision of Search becoming increasingly focused on helping customers accomplish tasks. Google Wallet aggregates data from linked accounts like Gmail and partner apps.

    Google Wallet affects travel (like airline tickets), finance, commerce, event tickets, plus sensitive data (in some regions) like drivers license, and health insurance cards. When this feature is enabled, Google Wallet automatically scans incoming emails to import boarding passes, event tickets, loyalty cards, and shipping updates.

    Now all of that is connected with Personal Intelligence.

    It has been revealed that connectivity to AI Mode is coming in the next few weeks. Google confirmed that connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence will enable AI Mode to pull information from across stored Google Drive documents, spreadsheets, and PDFs to provide personalized responses and assist consumers with projects, planning, and decision-making.

    “With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation strategy ahead of tax season.”.

    Industry observers note that personal Intelligence will be sharing Gemini conversational context between the Gemini app and AI Mode within the next few weeks. Search personalization will come in the form of more personally relevant responses based on recent search activity.

    Personalization transparency is coming soon. Customers will be able to see what personal context AI Mode used to generate a response and correct that information.

    Transformation Of Google Search Personal Intelligence represents a fundamental change in how Google Search (and/or AI Mode in Search) can respond to people, incorporating knowledge about their activities alongside information from the web.

    Unification Of Google’s Products And Services Previously disparate Google products and services are now increasingly part of a unified, personalized search experience.

    Google’s Agentic Layer The expansion of Personal Intelligence is consistent with Sundar Pichai’s vision of a unified, task-based experience that maintains context across Google’s products.

    Sharing Of Contextual Data The sharing of personal and conversational context across Google’s products enables users to continue activities without having to start over.

    Expansion Beyond Information Discovery The integration of additional data sources enables Google to become increasingly useful for planning, decision-making, and accomplishing tasks.

    Increasingly Personalized Search Experiences Search responses are becoming more specific to individual customers, a change that SEOs need to really think about and integrate into how what they do fits into this latest multi-dimensional level of Search.

    Recent findings suggest that how To Opt Out Of Google Personal Intelligence Google is giving people greater insight into and control over the personal context used to generate AI Mode responses. Users can opt out or in from Personal Intelligence here.

    Recent findings suggest that google Search is increasingly an experience that’s as much about what Google knows about the user and what they want to accomplish as it is about what the user is searching for. This is arguably one of the most consequential moments in SEO that I have experienced in my nearly 30 years of experience in SEO.

    RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a fresh website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney stated.

    According to recent reports, in Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website owners to our news coverage,” Eckenrode mentioned, and had some success with that strategy.

    In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in Latest York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    In a recent development, on the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” remarked Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a new California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    Meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a new book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As Engineering Manager for Recommender Systems, you'll lead the team that builds the backend retrieval and ranking infrastructure behind recommendations at Raya. You'll partner closely with the head of ML to drive our tech strategy and ensure our members get the best experience possible on the core surface of our product.

    We are looking for someone who is technically strong, has deep experience with production recommender systems, and has intuitive product-focused user empathy.

    We offer comprehensive medical and dental coverage, $50 a day food delivery budget, equity based employment, a great culture, learning opportunities, unlimited vacation, 12 weeks paid parental leave, and we pay all employees $1,000 a year to go somewhere in the world that they’ve never been because of our values of human connection, empathy, and curiosity.

    As Engineering Manager for Recommender Systems, you'll lead the team that builds the backend retrieval and ranking infrastructure behind recommendations at Raya. You'll partner closely with the head of ML to drive our tech strategy and ensure our members get the best experience possible on the core surface of our product.

    We are looking for someone who is technically strong, has deep experience with production recommender systems, and has intuitive product-focused user empathy.

    We offer comprehensive medical and dental coverage, $50 a day food delivery budget, equity based employment, a great culture, learning opportunities, unlimited vacation, 12 weeks paid parental leave, and we pay all employees $1,000 a year to go somewhere in the world that they’ve never been because of our values of human connection, empathy, and curiosity.

    Build, coach, and retain a high-performing backend team that specializes in recommender systems.

    Sources indicate that own reliable, low-latency production systems, observability, and incident response for recommendations. Catch regressions in latency, quality, or fairness before users notice.

    Create and execute a technical strategy that is grounded in deep product intuition and empathy for the end-user experience.

    Partner with the Machine Learning team to define roadmaps. Balance user-facing improvements with investments in infrastructure, reliability, and experimentation.

    Work with Data Science to co-own experimentation processes, tools, and best practices.

    3+ years managing engineers, with direct responsibility for hiring, performance management, career development, and delivery.

    Experience leading or building production recommender systems at scale.

    Hands-on depth in high-throughput, low-latency distributed systems that serve millions of users.

    Expertise in Go, Java/JVM, or a similar backend language; Postgres, and AWS/GCP, and Kubernetes.

    Experience with social networks or two-sided marketplaces in a subscription setting: you understand reciprocal interest, exposure, liquidity, and how great recommendations create long-term retentive value.

    Familiarity with how machine learning and AI fit into modern recommender systems.

    Experience with retrieval infrastructure such as Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, vector search, or feature stores.
